content: Acute pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition of the pancreas that is primarily characterized by abdominal pain and elevated levels of pancreatic enzymes in the bloodstream. This condition can arise from various causes and, depending on its severity, may lead to significant complications and high mortality rates despite appropriate treatment. The first clinical description of acute pancreatitis was provided by Nicholas Tulp, a Dutch anatomist, in 1652. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, significant contributions to the understanding of this condition were made by Reginald Fitz, Nicholas Senn, Eugene Opie, and others. These contributions continue to shape our current knowledge of acute pancreatitis. In 1901, Eugene Opie proposed the duct obstruction hypothesis, suggesting that obstruction of the pancreatic duct impairs pancreatic outflow, leading to pancreatitis. Later that same year, Opie introduced the common channel hypothesis, which posited that an impacted gallstone at the papilla of Vater creates a communication between the pancreatic and bile ducts, allowing bile to flow into the pancreatic duct and trigger pancreatitis. In 1963, the first Marseilles Symposium introduced a clinicopathologic classification of pancreatitis, which was revised in 1984 during the second Marseilles Symposium. In 1992, the Atlanta Symposium established a clinically based classification system for acute pancreatitis. Acute pancreatitis is classified into three categories: 1. Mild acute pancreatitis: This form is characterized by the absence of organ failure and local or systemic complications. 2. Moderately severe acute pancreatitis: This form involves transient organ failure (resolving within 48 hours) and/or local or systemic complications without persistent organ failure. 3. Severe acute pancreatitis: This form is defined by persistent organ failure, which may involve one or multiple organs. The pathophysiology of acute pancreatitis involves a loss of intracellular and extracellular compartmentalization, obstruction of pancreatic secretory transport, and activation of pancreatic enzymes. Once the disease is initiated, interstitial edema and inflammatory infiltration are hallmark features. The accumulation of polymorphonuclear granulocytes in pancreatic and extrapancreatic tissues, along with the release of leukocyte enzymes, plays a critical role in disease progression and the development of systemic complications. There are numerous causes of acute pancreatitis, including: Gallstones: The most common cause, accounting for 40–70% of cases. Alcohol: Responsible for approximately 25–35% of cases in the United States. Hypertriglyceridemia: Serum triglyceride levels above 1000 mg/dL (11 mmol/L) can precipitate acute pancreatitis, though lower levels may also contribute to disease severity. Hypertriglyceridemia accounts for 1–14% of cases. Post-ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography): Acute pancreatitis occurs in about 3% of patients undergoing diagnostic ERCP, 5% undergoing therapeutic ERCP, and up to 25% undergoing sphincter of Oddi manometric studies. Genetic factors: Patients with genetic predispositions may present with recurrent acute pancreatitis, childhood-onset pancreatitis without an identifiable cause, or progression to chronic pancreatitis. Medications: Drug-induced pancreatitis is rare, with an excellent prognosis and low mortality. Infections and toxins: Associated infections include: Viruses: Mumps, coxsackievirus, hepatitis B, cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster, herpes simplex, and HIV. Bacteria: Mycoplasma, Legionella, Leptospira, and Salmonella. Fungi: Aspergillus. Parasites: Toxoplasma, Cryptosporidium, and Ascaris. Other rare causes: Biliary sludge, microlithiasis, biliary obstruction, and hypercalcemia. Differentiating acute pancreatitis from other causes of epigastric abdominal pain is essential. Clinical features and laboratory studies help distinguish it from other conditions, such as: Peptic ulcer disease: Patients often have a history of intermittent epigastric pain that does not radiate to the back. Choledocholithiasis or cholangitis: Patients may have a history of gallstones or prior biliary manipulation, such as ERCP. Cholecystitis: Typically presents with abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium, which may radiate to the right shoulder or back. Perforated viscus: Presents with sudden-onset abdominal pain and peritoneal signs, such as guarding, rigidity, and rebound tenderness, which are not associated with acute pancreatitis. Intestinal obstruction: Patients may experience abdominal pain, anorexia, vomiting, obstipation or constipation, and elevated serum amylase and lipase levels.
